We all know that certain materials and products have to meet health standards and one thing and another. There may be no tariffs, and you may believe that there is free trade, but certain commodities are subject to health standards which in essence is a partial barrier. There is also a difference in the value of money, which creates another complexity in respect of trade.
I refer to the Barber commission report. When I began my remarks I said there was something I intended to tell the House that few members are aware of, and I shall do so now. I know of no other member of this House who presented a brief to the Barber commission on farm machinery costs. I submitted a brief to that commission outlining how I felt we could bring about lower farm machinery prices. I do not know of any other Member of Parliament who took the trouble to advise the commission on certain aspects of the farm machinery industry.
I have not been an advocate or a great promoter of Massey-Ferguson. If one studies the farm machinery inquiry carried out by the agricultural committee of the House of Commons he will discover that I was one of the worst interrogators of representatives of Massey-Ferguson.
You were always one of the worst.

The vice-president of Massey-Ferguson was beside himself because of the annoying questions I asked about their pricing set-up. That company charges all the market can bear, and there should be measures to bring about a realistic situation in respect of farm machinery prices. But we must allow the company to survive within Canada. It is one thing to bring about a realistic price mechanism within a company selling goods to Canadians but it is another thing to force an existing Canadian company out of Canada. It would still be selling at the same high prices in Canada.
Apparently the NDP wants to force Massey-Ferguson out of Canada and into the United States, and then let the company continue to sell at the high prices that now exist within Canada. That is not the solution to Canada's farm machinery problem. That is not a solution to the problem of unemployment within Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.
There is an opportunity for Canadian investment in the corporation in Canada, and it is a rather idealistic and foolish approach-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West seeks the floor on a point of order.
Are these strident exhortations an answer to my question, or is the hon. member launching a speech?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member asked the question and I think, with respect, he should not comment on the answer he gets.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member doth protest too much. My answer was too telling and he attempted to cut me off. The NDP wants to force through greater tax measures than those now proposed. In this way Massey-Ferguson will be forced out of Canada, with the hope that this will meet some NDP idealistic position. This company will still sell in Canada at the same high prices. This will not help our unemployment picture.
I would much rather encourage a Canadian international corporation such as Massey-Ferguson to remain in Canada, hiring Canadians and creating job opportunities. Then through corrective measures other than taxation we could encourage companies to sell their products at an acceptable rate, one that has some relationship to the value of the goods the machinery will be used to produce. This is what I would encourage Massey-Ferguson to do. The NDP is completely wrong if it believes in nationalization. If hon. members believe in nationalization, I wish they would all be like the hon. member for Waterloo who came out in favour of nationalization. They could then be judged on what they really believe, rather than on the camouflage they so often espouse.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope the hon. member for Crowfoot will forgive me if I do not follow in the vein in which he has been speaking this evening. I have listened to several hon. members of the Official Opposition take on my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo. So far as I am concerned they have not touched him, so I should like to discuss briefly a completely different phase of the general question of taxation of international income. Indeed, I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance will respond to the statement I wish to make and give the kind of assurance I am seeking on behalf of a large number of people.
While technically we are discussing section 2 of clause 1 of the bill, we are also discussing 18 or 20 other sections some of which have to do with the tax which must be paid by non-residents of Canada on income derived in Canada. Let me say quite clearly that we in this party welcome these provisions, particularly in so far as they endeavour to catch up with people who have taken their wealth to various tax havens around the world in order to avoid the payment of income tax either in Canada or anywhere else. It is no surprise, of course, to the parliamentary secretary when I say we agree with this aim as it is to be implemented in the bill before us.
However, in the attempt to make sure that all income earned in Canada is properly taxed, there are some specific provisions in this bill, and indeed in the sections under discussion now, about the taxation of pensions, superannuation benefits, annuities and other income of that kind. If I have read the bill correctly there is a provision that there should be a 25 per cent tax on most income of this kind. It is clear that old age security payments are exempt from any such 25 per cent tax, and there are a number of other pension benefits that are listed as not subject to this tax. However, it is also very clear that superannuation payments generally, payments
November 22, 1971

from the Canada Pension Plan, annuities, and so on, are subject to a 25 per cent tax.
I believe this is to be in the nature of a withholding tax so that before these payments are sent from Canada to persons living abroad the 25 per cent is to be deducted. The parliamentary secretary knows very well the kind of people I am thinking about, namely, pensioners who have gone to a more southern clime or to other parts of the world and are concerned when they learn of this 25 per cent withholding tax. Some of them say to me that the amount of income they have is such that they would not reach the 25 per cent level. But the bald way in which this is stated seems to fail to take that into account, and it also seems to ignore the exemption levels which apply to taxation in Canada.
I want to say quite clearly I have made inquiries. I have studied the various documents before us and I am satisfied that these people will not lose. In the first place, old age security pensions are not taxable in this way and in the final analysis the tax treaties which apply between Canada and other countries will come into play and in the end, even though there may have been a deduction at the source, no one who is retired and away from Canada living on a pension will pay any more income tax than he would have paid had he continued to live in Canada. Nevertheless, there is the bald and stark provision in this bill that there is a 25 per cent withholding tax on the total amount of certain kinds of pensions.
The parliamentary secretary realizes what I would like him to do. If he is able to get the floor now, I should like him to give a categorical assurance to public servants who retire, to people on annuities and to pensioners generally, that they need have no fear that by taking advantage of certain rights they have to go to another country that because of this 25 per cent withholding tax they will be in a worse position vis-a-vis their taxation than would have been the case had they remained in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first may I say it is most refreshing to return to something completely relevant and germane to the particular block of sections under discussion. Since the hon. member for Regina East asked me a question about NRO's earlier this afternoon, which I have not yet had an opportunity to answer, this is the first specific comment we have had on the sections before us.
I can give the hon. member the assurance he requests. The situation generally speaking is this: we do have treaties with certain countries. A proposal to impose a 15 per cent withholding tax, for example, in the case of a country like the United States does not override the existing treaty. Until and unless that treaty is changed, the provisions of the treaty will preclude that withholding tax being exacted. However, it is thought fair and equitable that in the circumstances Canada should have a right to withhold a tax. The hon. member will appreciate that the United States-since this is the example I have used-does tax income fully in the hands of the recipient resident of the United States.
The 25 per cent withholding tax is proposed in respect of other countries with which we do not have tax treaties at the moment. The legislation does give the Canadian taxpayer, the person from whom the 25 per cent is withheld, the option of filing a Canadian income tax return
Income Tax Act
and if as a result of filing that tax return the 25 per cent tax withheld in Canada means that he or she has paid more tax in total in Canada and in the foreign jurisdiction than would have been the case otherwise in either country, there would be a refund or credit against the tax allowed in Canada as a result of the taxpayer electing to file a Canadian income tax return.
Mr. Chairman, in listening to the hon. member for Fraser Valley West and the hon. member for Waterloo I was struck by the phoniness of the position customarily taken by hon. members to my left.
You said the same thing last year.

I did not say anything of the kind last year, but I am calling it phoniness now and I am calling it hypocrisy. It is out and out hypocrisy for an hon. member like the hon. member for Waterloo to spout socialistic concepts when he does not for a moment believe in them; and for the hon. member for Fraser Valley West to adopt the same spurious stance is just beyond comprehension.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I should like to correct the hon. member's pronunciation of the word "spurious".

The members of that party clutch taxes to their bosom like a suckling child. One would think that this offends the motherhood syndrome which they would have us believe the people of Canada believe they espouse. They want to appear to the people of the country-to the little man as they call him and as the Minister of Labour calls him-as champions of the little man. They think the more they put down the big corporations, the more votes they can get. This is absolutely shameful. I can understand why their noses are out of joint. In the last 31 years, at every turn they have been outmanoeuvered by the government. The hon. member for Crowfoot referred to creeping socialism. It is not creeping socialism at all; it is galloping completely out of control.
Hear, hear!

What are we to expect when we have at the helm the three horsemen of the Apocalypse sitting in the House, one upstairs in the Prime Minister's office, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, and the Secretary of State, all ex-members of the NDP? What are we to expect but galloping socialism?
Hear, hear!

We see the Leader of the NDP now, and before him the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands when he was leading that party, every time a government spokesman rises in his seat to announce some new measures, such as the Canada Development Corporation Act, the competition act or the investment incentives act, getting red in the face. They are burned up by their anger and by their indignation at being outmanoeuvered and pushed further out of the socialist spectrum. That is why they are angry. They cannot call themselves true socialists any more because they have been displaced. Nor can those across the way call themselves Liberals.

November 22, 1971
Income Tax Act
Hear, hear!

That is a pretty hollow claim. If they were to tell the truth and if they would banish this constant charade of parading themselves as Liberals, if they would banish hypocrisy and admit where this country is going with this list of legislation with which I will not bore the House, then we could have some truth in this place.
Oh, oh!

The hon. member for St. Boniface interjects over and over again with his loud mouth and loose tongue. If he would get up and participate in the debate he might give us the advantage of some of his views.
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman.
Oh, oh!

It would be very easy for one of us on the government side to rise and discuss matters sensibly with the opposition. But you will have noticed, Mr. Chairman, that the last speaker has not said one word pertaining to what we are discussing at present. All he has done is to criticize the NDP and the Liberals. So I suggest that if they-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. First, I will point out to the hon. member that the point he raised is not a question of privilege. However, I will also take this opportunity to tell the hon. member for Yukon that he should address himself to the Chair and should make his remarks relevant to section 2.

Mr. Chairman, I have never heard a larger pot than the hon. member for St. Boniface calling the kettle black. I hear him interjecting day after day. At least when I speak I have something to say, and that is more than I can say for the hon. member for St. Boniface.
Hear, hear!
The hon. member for Crowfoot-
Let us talk about St. Boniface for a while.
I do not think hon. members would agree to that. Unless the hon. member starts talking about it, the country will forget about St. Boniface.
Speak louder so I can hear you.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. It is difficult for the Chair to understand what is going on-I ask hon. members to help me keep order.
Eric, you are on.
For a moment I did not know whether the hon. member for St. Boniface had the floor or whether I had.
You do not know the difference. You are not here half the time.
One of these days he will have the courage to rise and tell us about his riding and his constituents, because we certainly have not heard anything yet.
It would make a hell of a lot more sense.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I will ask hon. members once more to give the Chair a chance to hear what is going on and to hear the speaker who has the floor. With their co-operation, I give the floor back to the hon. member for Yukon.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Crowfoot referred to timing. Indeed, this legislation is ill-timed. My urgings to the government have already been expressed by the hon. member for Crowfoot. Why are we in the difficulties that we face now with respect to the matters before us? This is a problem of the government's own making. How in the world can we expect the kind of economic climate to exist between ourselves and the United States when we have actions of the government such as we witnessed over the past few months, starting with the statement made in Russia by the Prime Minister referring to the U.S. military threat to Canada.
Oh, oh!
I hear groans from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. What I am saying is the truth, and the parliamentary secretary knows it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is the contrary.

It is not, and the parliamentary secretary knows it when he challenges my statement and says it is not correct. I am not the one who is lying. This was followed by the Premier of the Soviet Union, who came here and used Canada as a platform from which to make anti-American statements. That did not help. This followed on the heels of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources making a statement with respect to the investment of foreign money in this country for the purpose of constructing pipelines, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development travelling to the United States and making a statement diametrically opposed to that. No wonder the United States feels so confused.
Then, after cataloguing all these things, the Prime Minister says something is wrong and we have to mend the situation or at least give the appearance of mending it. So he calls together the offensive team, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and he shoves them across the country and instructs them to get the government out of the mess. What do they do? We find the Minister of Justice, whose portfolio has no concern with economics, saying in a speech to the Empire Club in Toronto last Thursday:
If there has been any straining in our friendship with the United States, that surely has resulted from Americans initiatives.
Having regard to statements of that nature from senior ministers of the Crown, how in the world are we going to smooth over the deterioration in our relations with the

November 22, 1971

United States which have never been so low in Canada's history.
Since Diefenbaker.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley West has interjected, "Since Diefenbaker."
Right.
That is an untrue, an uncalled for remark and it is beneath the dignity of the hon. member who uttered it. That former Prime Minister of this country was and is a great Canadian.

That is right. Mr. Chairman, I was accused of an untruth in regard to relationships between Canada and the United States. In response to the suggestion of the hon. member for Yukon that our relations were at a very low ebb, I suggested that they had not been at such a low ebb since the time of Right Hon. Prime Minister Diefenbaker. I do not retract that statement. I am suggesting that if they are not below that point now, that they are at least equal to it. It is not my problem; it is the problem of the hon. member for Yukon that this is so.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member knows that this is not a point of order. It is a matter of debate.
Does the hon. member wish to raise a point of privilege?
If you like.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. member have a point of order again?
Mr. Chairman, you suggested that my intervention was not a true point of order. If it would please Your Honour, I would change it to a point of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I said it was a matter of debate.

In all good conscience, if the hon. member for Fraser Valley West were called upon to answer he would have to admit he knew it was not a question of privilege but just another abuse of the rules to get an interjection on the record. In reply to the hon. member I say that it is not my problem. The situation in which we find ourselves today, with our relations with the United States being at the lowest ebb in our history, is the government's problem. If hon. members to my left were honest with themselves they would admit that.
You missed that debate.
I think I hear the hon. member for St. Boniface again.
You were away when that subject was discussed.
I wish the hon. member would speak up.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I just want to bring to the attention of the hon. member for Yukon that the matter he is discussing was
Income Tax Act
fully discussed in a debate when he was absent a couple of weeks ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Yukon.

I cannot understand how the hon. member for St. Boniface knows what was discussed in the House, because all he can hear is himself. In Toronto, the Minister of Justice-one of the offensive team-was followed by the Minister of Finance who, to put it mildly, has taken much buffeting in the last few months. In a speech there that minister said: "As it stands now the U.S. program contains elements that are prejudicial to the development of world trade." His whole speech was along that line. How on earth are we to improve rapidly deteriorating relations with a country that is so vital to our existence by sending out ministers to say that kind of thing?
On top of these harsh, blunt, undiplomatic statements made by ministers of the Crown-and the Prime Minister is no exception-we have things like the leakage of the Gray report advising of the setting up of some kind of screening mechanism, staffed by a board with broad, sweeping powers to exercise political discretion over what foreign capital can come into this country, how much of it, for where, and for what purpose. Members of the NDP would dearly love to see that happen. I point out that the so-called pseudo Liberals have been stealing the stuff of the NDP for as long as I can recall. That is why members of the NDP are now redundant. The true NDP are all over there opposite me. Why don't you go over there? That is where you belong. Conversely, the government should move over to this side.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I ask the hon. member to address himself to the Chair.

Mr. Chairman, I have been careful about addressing my remarks through the Chair, but because I may have been facing in another direction this does not mean that I have forgotten about Your Honour's existence. Then one must read some of the editorial comment on this subject.
More questions.
The hon. member for St. Boniface is disgruntled again.
All you can do is read quotations from newspapers.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The Chair is having a very difficult time tonight. This is my worst experience so far in the chair. I am trying to follow everything that is said. I wish hon. members would allow the hon. member for Yukon to speak without interruption so that I may follow what he is saying.

Mr. Chairman, I am greatly interested in the interjections of the hon. member for St. Boniface. They merely point out the great unrest that exists in the backbenches on the opposite side. This is one way for the hon. member to blow off a little steam. I don't begrudge it to him because he needs it, if only to maintain good health.

November 22, 1971
Income Tax Act
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I just want to say that I agree with the hon. member that there is unrest here, but it is because we are getting tired of listening to nothing.

I think the hon. member will agree with me that for 31 years we have been listening to nothing from the government backbenches. In an editorial last Saturday the Globe and Mail said:
Even the hesitation of business to invest deplored by Mr. Benson has its Canadian causes-the long doubt of the tax bill, the dangerous and arbitrary elements of the competition act, and now the foreshadowing of another arbitrary tribunal in the Gray report.
There, Sir, is the nub of the question. The problems the government is facing today are problems of its own creation, because of its blind, stubborn, stupid ineptness in managing the country, as a result of which it now finds itself deep in the proverbial mire. The editorial added:
Verbal assaults on the United States will not solve our problems. Even U.S. concessions would not solve them all. Our economic disease has its Canadian causes, which can only be removed by new Canadian initiatives.
We are not going to see any initiatives coming from the government or coming from the NDP, because all they are concerned about is one great superstructure of the state having control over virtually every aspect of our freedoms, our freedoms of commerce, of industry, of business, and in that respect members of the NDP are beaten hollow by those who sit on the government benches.
Hear, hear!
They can cry in their soup until doomsday because until the government goes they will be outlefted every time-and heaven help us if the government doesn't go soon.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks in connection with Bill C-259 and the portion which we are supposed to be discussing. Perhaps I should say that we are talking about the taxation policy on income, as it applies to Canadian individuals and Canadian corporations, from foreign sources. I happen to belong to a group of people which I hope is not in the minority, people who are pleased and proud of the fact that in Canada we do have corporations large enough to compete in all the markets of the world.
Hear, hear!

This business of trying to point the finger at corporations that have their head office in Canada, as though it were a crime, does not stand up in my opinion and should be frowned upon by every member of this assembly.
Hear, hear!

We are discussing a complex phase of a complex portion of the tax reform bill. When I say tax reform I want to say that I do not subscribe to the words whatsoever, because tax reform suggests tax improvement. This is not tax improvement by any stretch of the imagination. If people were honest with themselves they

would not call this monstrosity tax improvement, because it is not.
When the bill is referred to committee of the whole then I suggest it is the business of the minister sponsoring it to be in his place to explain the bill for the illumination of all members. In this case, that responsibility has been delegated to the parliamentary secretary to the minister, the hon. member for Calgary South, and I find no fault with that. But when the parliamentary secretary fails to rise in his place at the beginning of any series of sections of a complex bill to explain to the committee what the government expects to accomplish by these new portions of this bill, then I do find fault.
They don't know yet.

If you will examine the bill you will see that in every case it is written that these are new sections. I submit it was the duty of the parliamentary secretary to rise in his place and explain why the changes are being made and what gain is expected in comparison to the old act. As I said a few moments ago, while I do not agree with the principle of delegation because people are elected for a specific purpose, since it had to be done I am sure it could not be on more capable shoulders-except that he did not do it. He has not given the committee any explanation of why this is done and what the government expects to gain by it.
I shall give a bit of information on what we are gaining under the present act. Let us examine the record, Mr. Chairman, and see what it shows. We find that in 1970 Canada received $513 million in interest and dividends on foreign holdings, a 74 per cent increase over the 1967 revenue of $295 million. In 1967, Canadian direct investment abroad represented a book value of $4 million out of total long-term investments with a book value of a little over $8 million. Canadian direct investment abroad in 1970 was $215 million exclusive of undistributed profits.
With that in mind, Mr. Chairman, it becomes the duty of the parliamentary secretary to tell this House what improvement the government is going to make. I know what has been said by some members. They have raised this particular phase of the new bill and emphasized that portion of it which would interfere with people who are wealthy and move their place of residence to another country. I agree with that. I do not, however, agree with the idea of saying to Canadian corporations which are doing business throughout the world that you are going to make it as hard as you can for them because there are ways in which they could be made to pay taxes.
In my opinion, the people who are contributing to taxation in this country, which last year amounted to something in the area of $6 billion or $7 billion, are a most important class because they contribute to the expense of various social services and the expense of government in general. Why should the government try to make it hard for the taxpayer? It seems to me that what they are doing is discouraging him or the corporation to the extent that he loses his incentive to go ahead and make a profit. I happen to believe in profit because, in the first place, I believe it makes for good times and, in the second place, government gets about 50 per cent of it anyway. I see that you agree, Mr. Chairman, because you smile. Why should the taxpayer be held up almost as a public enemy of

November 22, 1971

Canada when he is almost the greatest benefactor that the country could possibly have?
I think we have to look at all these phases, but it seems to me that the government has not considered them. They seem determined to make change, but unless you can make an improvement you should not make change. The power to tax is surely the power to destroy, and the power to change taxes and make them more onerous surely has the same connotation. I think the parliamentary secretary should have been on his feet a long time ago telling this House what the government had in mind and why they were doing it.
He doesn't know.

Mr. Chairman, I believe that the remark of my hon. friend from the Yukon is correct; I do not think they know. They do not seem to know, but they seem to have the idea that they must of necessity make changes. It really amounts to this. The government thinks it must make changes for the sake of change. That is all we have here.
Mr. Chairman, I make this assertion: income from foreign affiliates is not at present taxed by Canada when it is earned or remitted as dividends; only when that income is distributed by the Canadian parent company to the shareholders will it become taxable, presumably. In other words, the government is making it impossible for a company with an affiliate in another country to bring funds from that affiliate into Canada without paying tax. It cannot bring money into its own treasury even. That seems to be a step in the wrong direction. We must look at possible government objectives for clues to indicate why the government is thinking this way. I have referred to the question of tax havens.
Are you for or against them?

The government's objective may be to allow Canadian businesses operating abroad to remain competitive and viable. Mr. Chairman, you cannot make them competitive and viable if you impose on them provisions like these so that they cannot live. That, to me, does not seem sensible. There has been talk of bilateral tax treaties. These treaties are not easily made. They take a great deal of time. Why, for goodness sake, is it necessary to enter into additional tax treaties when under the present law $513 million in cash flowed into the treasury of this country in 1970? In 1971 it is quite possible that the amount will be much greater. The international aspects of Bill C-259, Mr. Chairman, might be described as a nightmare of overkill, subverting international equity and confronting Canada's international interests with grim prospects.
I think the parliamentary secretary should explain what the government has in mind. Why did 44 top businessmen come to Ottawa today, if not to express concern about the new tax legislation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
They came because they were invited by the Prime Minister.
Income Tax Act

So the Prime Minister invited them. Let us accept that as a proper statement. But why are they here, if not to object? I submit that business in Canada today is in a state of tremendous confusion and uncertainty resulting largely from the government's actions on taxation. The government seems determined to make change for the sake of change. It has not been demonstrated to me that things needed to be improved.
I said a moment ago that about $6 billion of our total revenue, or about 50 per cent, comes from the taxation of individuals and corporations. However, I did not give the whole story and now I want to do so. In the three years for which I am about to give figures-that is, 1968, 1969 and 1970-the revenue from taxation under the headings I referred to was $4.5 billion, $5.3 billion and $6.7 billion respectively. The point is that here we have tax laws which apparently without disturbing the business community resulted in increased revenues every year of about $1 billion. The government is not satisfied with that; apparently it wants more.
The plain fact is that if business in Canada and abroad is to remain competitive, it must operate in a tax environment that is at least as favourable as that applying to its foreign competitors. I should like the parliamentary secretary to listen to me. If businesses are to remain competitive, Mr. Chairman, it is necessary for them to operate in a tax environment that is no less favourable than that in which their foreign competitors operate. That seems like ordinary, common sense. Apparently this government is not conscious of that fact or, if it is, it is absolutely indifferent. They go merrily on their way chasing after the last dollar and trying to portray the businesses of this country as public enemy No. 1. That is what the government is doing by this legislation.
Ten o'clock.

I will take only a minute, Mr. Chairman. We have no assurance from the government that the restrictive measures which have been included in this bill will have any beneficial effect. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would like to convince me that they will. I would be glad to be convinced. So far, however, I remain unconvinced. The government seems to be absolutely unconscious of the effects of high taxation. It is time it woke up and considered what action it ought to take in the interests of all the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte was the first member of the official opposition who displayed any interest in the contents of this particular block of sections. I only regret that he took up all the time available and that I cannot respond to him.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I wish to draw your attention to the fact that some electronic equipment has been used in the committee. I should like the Chair to rule on whether that is a proper procedure for the hon. member for Davenport to follow.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I do not see any
equipment.

Look. It is in his hand.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INDIA-REQUEST TO SEND DRIED POTATOES TO AID IN FOOD SHORTAGE
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INDIA-REQUEST TO SEND DRIED POTATOES TO AID IN FOOD SHORTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I raised this issue some time ago it was because of my hope that something additional might be found to add to the assistance this country and its people are providing for the unfortunate refugees in the Indian subcontinent. While there are events, political problems and grave dangers of serious international consultations, the human problem is urgent, pressing and compelling.
I do not hesitate, and I never have hesitated, to endorse enthusiastically the efforts of this country to assist developing countries and, more particularly, to assist the nationals of other countries in time of unique and special need. Certainly, the last requirement is met in the tragedy which has befallen the millions of people who have fled East Pakistan for India. The world must know that the Indian burden is immense and must be taxing the capacity of that country, and thus we cannot overlook any avenue of assistance.
It is one of the sad anomalies of our world that some parts are in abundance and others are in grave deficiency, even confining ourselves to foodstuffs. It passes the understanding of most people that we find some areas of the world with food that is wasted and other parts of the world where people literally starve. This was a perplexing problem in the thirties in the Canadian prairies, and I suppose the American prairies too. Wheat was burned or roasted to make a form of coffee, while in Brazil coffee was destroyed because there was no sale. Canadians could have used the coffee and the Brazilians could have used the wheat, but never could we get the proper correlation between surplus and deficiency.
It would seem that in our highly sophisticated age when we can literally land on the moon and send with precision the most sophisticated instruments to the planet Mars, there must be something wrong in our universal patterns of life if we cannot relate the terrible needs of some human beings to the overproduction of others.
I know that respect must be had for the life styles and taste preferences of people, and I understand that we have in the past made mistakes and sent food to areas where the people either could not or would not make use of it. However, it is my understanding that dried, instant potatoes can be usefully added to the diet of the East Pakistan refugees. As I understand it, a mixture of these potatoes with spices, combined with some leafy vege-

tables which are found in the area, add considerably to the rations of these people.
One of the great problems which faced the sector of the agricultural industry devoted to potatoes is the fact that this crop was perishable and, unlike wheat, could not be stored from year to year. The advent of the potato flake, instant potatoes-a most wonderful product-has helped to make this problem a little less acute.
My main concern in this question is not to criticize but to inquire as to what has been done by the Department of External Affairs, by CIDA, what advice has been received from the Department of Agriculture on the possibility of making use of the ample supplies of potatoes in an instant form to assist in providing sustenance for the unfortunates in India. I hope the parliamentary secretary will be able to indicate that considerable research has been done and that the omens are good for this further development of Canada's external aid program.
I still believe that the best possible contribution is cash-cold, hard and generously delivered cash-but foodstuffs that are light and therefore reasonably easy to transport should be utilized wherever possible. I call upon the government to make every effort toward the utilization of these items. I note with immense concern and profound sorrow what was said by our representative at the United Nations the other day, reporting what the UNHCR man had reported to the United Nations assembly, namely, that it would require $700 million to provide for the basic needs of these refugees for the year ending March, 1972.
I profoundly hope, with a great feeling that we must all unite on this matter, that something can be done in this particular area in order to provide some amelioration of the terrible need of so many of our fellow human beings who are experiencing great distress and unique suffering.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INDIA-REQUEST TO SEND DRIED POTATOES TO AID IN FOOD SHORTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we fully share the sympathy of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) on the question presently under study.
His opinion is also shared by the government but I must tell him, on that matter, that the Canadian International Development Agency has been approached and encouraged to provide Pakistan refugees in India with instant dehydrated potatoes.
Senior officials of the agency have consulted representatives of the FAO and the League of Red Cross Societies and both inquiries have clearly demonstrated that dehydrated potatoes do not meet the dietetic needs of this population and that this moreover implied serious difficulties due to the rudimentary implements available in that country. However, CIDA officials are still seeking the best way of utilizing the stocks that have already been shipped by various private organizations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue I wish to speak about briefly this evening is
November 22, 1971

concerned with the degree of effort this government is making to provide our trading partners, more particularly the United States of America, with information directly relevant to current issues that exist between our two countries. The question is by no means an abstract one; quite the contrary. I was in Washington last week to speak with representatives of both the legislative and executive branch of that government in connection with the Canada-United States automotive agreement. To my dismay I discovered that those at the legislative level were simply uninformed of Canada's position and the facts-I emphasize "the facts"-concerning the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement.
I spoke with Senators Buckley and Gravel, the former from New York city and the latter from Alaska, concerning an amendment that they had put before the U.S. Senate a week ago Saturday. The substance of the amendment was extremely important to this country. If passed, it would have recommended to the President of the United States that that government exempt both Canada and Mexico from the current surcharge. The vote failed by seven votes only. In other words, if four Senators had voted the other way, that amendment would have passed.
The central argument used against the exemption of Canada came from Senator Long, chairman of the important finance committee, and it stressed almost exclusively the so-called reneging by Canada on the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement. The Senators present who were supporting the amendment simply did not have at their disposal, so I am informed and have had partially confirmed, contrary facts, facts that could and should have been provided to them by our embassy in the United States.
I am not arguing or suggesting strong tactics or anything of that kind, but simple, straightforward provision of information to important and powerful politicians should have been carried out. The minister in his reply to my question in the House this afternoon as to the degree of action we took in this area, suggested this was perhaps inappropriate. He said it was perhaps permitted both by our government and others but it might cause more harm than good. It seems to me that anyone who knows anything at all about the operation of modern government could not accept this answer at face value. Virtually all active governments are busy providing us as Members of Parliament on a regular and daily basis with all kinds of information concerning themselves. We are ordinary Members of Parliament and, indeed, almost half of us are members of the opposition. It seems to me that in the United States system of government the legislative branch is in many basic ways much more powerful compared with Members of Parliament.
This is all the more reason for saying it is an essential function of our embassy abroad and the foreign policy of this government to keep people at that legislative level in the United States government informed of Canadian positions, and particularly informed of basic factual information that could be used in a positive way when votes are taken in the Senate or in Congress which could have a good or detrimental effect on this country.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
To repeat the point, the vote last Saturday could well have been different and could well have come out in Canada's favour if members of our embassy and members of this government had been doing the job they ought to have been doing.

It is of course one of the
responsibilities of our embassy in Washington to establish contact with all sectors of the United States government. Officers are expected to be acquainted with not only their opposite numbers in the administration but also with Senators and Congressmen who are interested in Canadi-an-Ameriean relations.
Several Senators supported the unsuccessful amendment to the tax bill, advocating withdrawal of the 10 per cent surcharge from Canada and Mexico. Many of them may have been made aware of the general Canadian position, including the auto pact, and of the effects of the surcharge on our economy, through the efforts of our Washington embassy staff. Such contact between diplomats and legislators within the country to which diplomats are accredited is normal and natural. Indeed, officers might be subject to criticism if they did not develop and maintain these contacts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, November 19, as reported at page 9713 of Hansard, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister to give consideration to a problem that has arisen as a result of the royalties being collected by the Authors, Publishers and Composers Association of Canada for the use of "O Canada" when played at any time by any organization which charges admission. Up to the present time "God Save the Queen" and "O Canada" have been accepted as national anthems. This organization, this all-powerful behemoth of art, have a copyright on "O Canada". Will the Prime Minister give consideration to bringing before Parliament the necessary legislation to cancel the copyright as such a preposterous anachronism whereby Canadians have to pay for the privilege of having "O Canada" played?
In reply, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that it was the intention of the government to bring in legislation on this matter but that it will not be possible at this session. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. member for Prince Albert is badly mistaken in his facts. The copyright for "O Canada" was turned over to the Crown in October, 1969, for the sum of $1. I am in possession of photostat copies of letters indicating that this offer was made on a number of previous occasions by Gordon V. Thompson Limited, who held the copyright.

speechtext:
I will ignore the remarks. As I say, I have photostatic documents, and I trust the hon. member making the objection is in possession of material to back up the very false statement he made in his interjection. I am in possession of photostats of letters indicating that the offer was made on a number of previous occasions by Gordon V. Thompson Limited, who held the copyright. While this firm is a member of the Authors, Publishers and Composers Association of Canada, such nominal royalties as were collected were actually collected by Gordon V. Thompson Limited.
My purpose in raising the matter at this time is to clear the name of Mr. Gordon V. Thompson, in the interests of his family some of whom reside in Ottawa. While a student at the University of Toronto before the First World War, the late Mr. Thompson became interested in the lyrics of "O Canada" in English. Some 40 versions were current at that time. After much research and consultation with many authorities, he finally came to the conclusion that the version by Judge Robert Stanley Weir of Montreal was the most generally accepted.
The problem of how to protect the lyrics of a song which had no official status but which many hoped would become the national anthem was a difficult one. Mr. Thompson negotiated with the heirs of Judge Weir and took out a copyright. By means of the copyright he and his firm were able to protect the dignity of the lyrics and the music as something which they could pass on to future generations.
In the course of administering the copyright a number of difficult decisions arose. In one case a parody of the song was prepared and, of course, this was forbidden. In another case a firm wanted to make a singing commercial to sell deodorants, using the music of "O Canada", which was again refused. While these cases were obviously offensive to public taste, other decisions were much harder to make. In general, permission to use the copyright was granted freely for any public or non-profit purpose.
As far as royalties were concerned, I am informed that these amounted to approximately $150 per year, of which 50 per cent was turned over to the estate of Judge Weir. A royalty of 10 cents per sheet for sheet music produced negligible returns, but all the money from this source was turned over to Judge Weir's estate. The costs of administering the copyright, of preventing abuse and maintaining uniformity of the version across Canada, indeed for international purposes, far exceeded the nominal royalties received. Indeed, the firm of Gordon V. Thompson Limited became specialists in this kind of work. They were given responsibility for administering the copyright of Canada's centennial song written by Bobby Gimbey, and also I believe they have a similar arrangement with the "Ontario" song promoted by the province of Ontario.
A review of correspondence in my hands indicates that Mr. Thompson offered on a number of occasions to turn over his copyright to the Crown, which was finally done in
1969.	The task of working out a fair set of rules to guide those responsible for administration of the copyright, however, has not yet been completed by the Secretary of State's department. No doubt in the near future we can expect, as the Prime Minister indicated, legislation and possibly regulations to deal with this complex and difficult subject.
Those interested in the subject might refer to the 1967 report of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on the National and Royal Anthems, and the Minutes of Proceedings of November 30, 1967, pages 55-58. It is to the credit of the late Gordon V. Thompson that he undertook to copyright the Weir version of "O Canada" in order to protect it as a public service. Through the device of the copyright, a standard version was promoted from coast to coast and the other versions have fallen into disuse. The fact that the Weir version has received the recognition it enjoys today is in no small part due to Mr. Thompson's efforts and it is out of a sense of obligation to set the record straight that I have taken the opportunity of raising this matter tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. Barnett J. Danson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):

speechtext:
The statement made by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the press article on which it was based were both inaccurate. The Composers, Authors and Publishers Association of Canada requires royalties for their repertory, and "O Canada" is not included in this repertory.
So far as the English version is concerned, "O Canada" copyrights have been Crown property since October 12,
1970,	at which time the heirs of Judge Weir, I am given to understand, through selfless effort and the co-operation of Gordon Thompson turned over to the government the copyrights. The French version, both the words and the music, have been public property for a number of years.
